entities.name: Guillaume Fichet
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Guillaume Fichet (1433–c. 1480) was a French theologian, rhetorician, and university official who, with Johann Heynlin (Jean Heynlin de Stein), brought the first printing press to France at the Sorbonne in Paris (1470). A prior of the Sorbonne and doctor of theology, Fichet championed humanist rhetoric and saw typography as a tool for reforming preaching, learning, and the circulation of classical and theological texts. The Paris press issued Latin works that signalled France’s entry into the Gutenberg revolution only fifteen years after Mainz.

Fichet’s importance is both technological and cultural: he linked university scholastic institutions to the new medium, ensuring that print in France began under academic–clerical auspices rather than only commercial workshops. His collaboration with Heynlin and German printers illustrates how skills migrated from the Rhine to Paris. Though he later left for Italy and the press’s early phase was brief, the 1470 Sorbonne workshop inaugurated a Parisian print culture that soon became one of Europe’s densest.
